items.title: An honour or a burden? What to know if you've agreed to settle a loved one's estate
items.description: People often name someone they love and trust to be executor of their estates, which involves settling debts, managing assets and tying up loose ends.
items._ogDesc: People often name someone they love and trust to be executor of their estates, which involves settling debts, managing assets and tying up loose ends.
items.body:
All things considered, Julia Chung had a lot working in her favour when she was tasked with settling the estates of not one, but two, uncles who died earlier this year.

As a financial planner, she has more money know-how than most. And her uncles had each clearly communicated their end-of-life wishes and ensured vital information was accessible.

Even still, it’s been exhausting.

“When you’re experiencing grief at the same time, which I definitely have been, there were moments where I was like, ‘I literally can’t think,’” Chung, CEO of Spring Planning, said in an interview from Vancouver.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

People often name someone they love and trust to be executor of their estates, which involves settling debts, managing assets and tying up myriad other loose ends. It’s a time-consuming, emotionally heavy and logistically dizzying role that can sometimes bring a financial hit. Those agreeing to take on this duty should have a clear-eyed understanding of what it entails and an openness to sharing some of the load, experts say.

“This is hundreds of hours of work,” said Erin Bury, co-founder of estate planning firm Willful. “This is not a minor task, and it involves a lot of co-ordination and expertise that you may not possess.”

Expect the whole process to take at least a year — maybe much longer.

Responsibilities in the immediate aftermath include making arrangements for the body, and any funeral or celebration of life. Executors need to get copies of the death certificate and track down the original will. They also need to secure the deceased’s property — changing locks and making sure insurance doesn’t lapse.

Later, there’s communicating with beneficiaries, getting in touch with banks and service providers and filing final tax returns.

Executors should be prepared to go through probate, a legal process where a court deems the will valid and gives the executor the authority to carry it out, though it doesn’t apply in all cases.

Until probate is complete and funds from the estate can be unlocked, an executor may have to front the cost of the funeral, lawyers, accountants and bills that still need to be paid.

Executors are entitled to compensation for their time. If the amount isn’t set out in the will, there are limits under provincial legislation.

The job comes with a fiduciary duty to act in the best interest of the estate’s beneficiaries.

“There’s a legal obligation to manage the assets and pay off the liabilities of the estate in a manner that doesn’t waste the assets. If the estate is going to take a long time to administer, you need to make sure that the investment portfolio is managed correctly, you’re taking reasonable steps to ensure the safety of all of the assets,” said Mark Biderman, senior vice-president of trust and legal at Cidel Private Bank, which provides executor and other services.

An insolvent estate opens up a whole new host of challenges for executors.

“If creditors need to be paid, typically (executors) are the ones holding the bag at the end of the day,” said Biderman.

There can also be complications when the executor lives in a different jurisdiction than the deceased. An executor might have to put up assets as collateral in order to act if they’re out of province. And if the assets are outside Canada, there’s another country’s laws to navigate.

ClearEstate, a tech-based estate planning and settlement company, recently commissioned a poll that suggested Canadians have contradictory feelings about enlisting a loved one as executor.

Nine in 10 respondents said being an executor can be a complicated and time-consuming job that most people aren’t prepared for. But three quarters said they’d accept the assignment if asked. Nearly two-thirds agreed it’s not fair to expect a family member to handle it on their own.

“It’s not a gift. People take it as an honour and take it as a sign of trust, but the reality is it’s a huge burden,” said ClearEstate CEO and co-founder Davide Pisanu.

A lot of the heavy lifting has to be done during limited business hours.

“There’s a massive tax on society through this process because you’re very often taking people in their 50s and 60s who are still working — sometimes even younger, they have young kids — and then they’re stuck with this massive admin burden of unwinding a loved one’s estate, which is brutal,” said Pisanu.

Saying no is an option. So too is backing out years down the line when life circumstances have changed; in that case, a backup executor could step in if one is named in the will or it goes to the courts. Financial firms can be hired to take the lead on all the bureaucracy and paperwork, with the cost drawn from the estate.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The experts agree it’s worthwhile to sit down with your loved one before they pass to go over where their will is, who they bank with, where their passwords can be found and other crucial information.

And for those stepping into the role, Chung said record keeping should be immaculate, both because memory can falter in the fog of grief and because of the sheer volume of tasks to keep track of. Keep receipts. Jot down who you’ve spoken to and about what.

But mostly, Chung advises executors to take it one step at a time.

“It’s really stressful, especially if you care very much about the person that you just lost,” she said. “Just try to map out what’s urgent, what isn’t urgent, what absolutely needs me, what things can I potentially outsource, what can I put off for a little bit?”

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
items.body:
TEL AVIV, Israel — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.

With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.

“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.

He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.

Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”

Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region

Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.

The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.

October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.

Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.

Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks

Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.

Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.

Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.

The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped keep oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.

Iran says it’s open to diplomacy but also self-defence

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said that a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.

Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. In recent days, Tehran has indicated that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.

The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.

Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.

Iran still promotes its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.

In late September, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.

The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes

A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.

The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.

Now the landscape of the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.

The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.

The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.

By Melanie Lidman, The Associated Press

items.title: Uranium sector offers compelling investment case: Brooke Thackray
items.description: The uranium sector has a strong fundamental profile for long-term growth.

items._ogDesc: The uranium sector has a strong fundamental profile for long-term growth.
items.body:
The uranium sector has a very strong fundamental profile to move higher over the long term, and demand is expected to continue to grow. Nuclear power is now considered a source of green energy and the world’s demand for energy is skyrocketing.

The buildout of AI and the shift to electrically powered transportation have created new sources of demand for electricity.

“Electricity is at the heart of modern economies and electricity demand grows much faster than overall energy use in all scenarios. It rises by around 40 per cent to 2035 in both the CPS and the STEPS, and by more than 50 per cent in the NZE Scenario,” according to IEA World Energy Outlook 2025.

Supply is not expected to be able to keep up with demand and is expected to decline. It takes 10 to 15 years to greenfield (develop from scratch) a uranium mine. Even if more uranium mines were started today, the output would not come online for many years to come. Most analysts and experts in the field acknowledge that there is going to be a substantial shortfall in uranium production. It is just a matter of how much of a shortfall and when it occurs.

The graph below illustrates two different scenarios of world uranium production capability compared to nuclear reactor requirements. One is a low-production scenario (left) and the other a high-production scenario. In either case, there is a shortfall of uranium production.

Investing in the uranium sector in the stock market has been a frustrating experience. Although the price of uranium stocks has risen over the last few years, the uranium sector has moved lower since January 2026. This has happened as a number of positive announcements for the nuclear industry have been released in 2026.

One of the reasons that the price of uranium has not risen rapidly, despite increasing demand and positive announcements, is that uranium mining companies have been reopening dormant mines. This option has been quickly dissipating as the nuclear mining industry has been increasingly using up its spare capacity.

The uranium sector in the stock market has been moving lower since January of this year. Below is a graph of the performance of the Global X Uranium ETF (URA) that trades on the NYSE. It is a proxy for the uranium sector. The sector is down 16.8 per cent YTD and is down 42.5 per cent since its January high (as of end of day October 21).

The sector has become dramatically oversold on a number of metrics. The uranium sector typically performs well on a seasonal basis in November through January. If the broad stock market manages to perform well in the near future, it would be reasonable to expect the uranium sector to also perform well and outperform the S&P 500.

Although the uranium sector has been moving lower in the stock market, the long-term contract price (term) of uranium has been moving higher. The red line in the graph below represents the long-term contract price of uranium as posted by Cameco on its website.

It is clear that the term contract price has been moving higher over the last few years, including 2026. The black line represents the spot price of uranium, which the market tends to focus on. The spot price has been more volatile than the long-term price. As shown in the graph, when the spot price is below the term price and the term price is rising, the spot price tends to play catch-up and also rises.

If the term contract price continues its trend higher, it is reasonable to expect the spot price to also rise. A rising spot price will be supportive of the uranium sector in the stock market.

Investors find it hard to reconcile how the uranium sector could have such a positive profile with the falling price of the uranium sector in the stock market. Most investors have the uranium sector as a lower priority in their investment choices. The supply is known over the next few years as well as the demand, and as a result, investors have chosen to focus on other parts of the market, such as AI.

The problem with ignoring the compelling case for the uranium sector is that when things change, the sector can move rapidly higher. It is difficult to predict when a catalyst may force a rapid revaluation for the uranium sector. In 2024 and 2025, the sector moved higher because of the overwhelming number of positive announcements that were favourable for uranium. Governments were announcing the creation of stockpiles and special programs to support the uranium industry. Hyperscalers were announcing deals to use nuclear power to power their AI data centres.

Positive news releases for uranium are released almost daily. When the next slew of really big announcements will be released is not known. It can happen at any time. A constantly rising term contract price of uranium is supportive for the sector to move higher. The sector has become very oversold on a number of metrics and is poised to move higher. The case for investing in the uranium sector has become very compelling.

items.description: Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May because of worries about the war with Iran.

items._ogDesc: Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging down markets worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May because of worries about the war with Iran.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 tumbled 1.4 per cent following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Nasdaq composite was down 2.2 per cent, as of 10:45 a.m. Eastern time, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 0.6 per cent, or 295 points.

AI-related stocks have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 9.7 per cent.

It gave a range as its forecast for profit in the final three months of 2026 whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4 per cent surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment.

Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 6.4 per cent after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla erased an early drop to rise 0.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 3.8 per cent. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 7.1 per cent, though it’s swung between gains and losses of roughly 4 per cent in each of the last two days.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7 per cent.

Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6 per cent to US$111.60 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the US$97 to US$112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1 per cent It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big debt affect almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors.

But U.S. yields nevertheless sank Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.01 per cent from 5.13 per cent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. That’s a notable move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could be a signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, though they got drowned out by the drops for the more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.8 per cent.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

items.title: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
items.description: Some of the key data centres at the heart of Russia's technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[This satellite image taken by Planet Labs PBC on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 shows a data center which was severely damaged by an Oct. 8 Ukrainian drone strike, in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region of Russia. (Planet Labs PBC via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Uncredited</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Some of the key data centres at the heart of Russia's technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion.
items.body:
Russia prides itself on its digital advances — from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence.

But now, some of the key data centres at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair.

Ukraine this month hit three main data centres belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country’s equivalent to Facebook.

While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex’s virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The fallout even spread to Russia’s judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access.

Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow’s aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back.

“This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group.

Data centres have been hit by both sides in the war

Data centres are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other’s vital infrastructure.

Russian missiles and drones have pummeled Ukraine’s power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of U.S.-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington’s war with Iran.

Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians.

U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the U.S. war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies.

Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia’s top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon.

Kyiv’s attacks on Russian data centres closely followed Moscow’s recent strikes on data centres in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts.

On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data centre in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers. A data centre in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11.

The data centre and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data centre in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte.

Data centres are vulnerable

While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centres are even softer targets — massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives.

The vulnerability of data centres was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them.

Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centres, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn’t immediately clear why air defenses near the sites had failed.

“The problem in Russia is that they’ve got to cover a big country with air defense and they don’t have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group.

Russia’s efforts to build a ‘sovereign internet’ backfire

Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow’s strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable.

“Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it’s relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said.

Klimarev predicted the data centre attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage.

“Paradoxically, the strikes on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It’s quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.”

Russians are vexed by service disruptions

Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. It provides a wide variety of functions, including a search engine, cloud storage, payment apps, geolocation and ride-hailing services, and e-commerce platforms.

“Yandex is kind of like Uber and Amazon and Google and everything rolled into one,” with everything “concentrated in just a few data centres,” Reiners said. “From a strategic perspective, they’re an excellent target.”

The attacks on Yandex caused unprecedented disruptions, paralyzing payments, online orders, taxi rides and access to personal data.

Moscow resident Igor Mann said he couldn’t collect an order he placed with Yandex Market, an e-commerce platform. He said he tried using a virtual private network, but “nothing worked.”

Taxi driver Pavel Belyavskiy, who gets orders via Yandex’s ride-hailing app, couldn’t connect with passengers.

“On several orders already, I’ve ended up waiting for a long time and had to cancel the ride because I couldn’t even get in touch with the passenger,” he said.

The attacks also caused temporary disruptions at some major companies and banks that rely on Yandex cloud services.

“It’s not just about convenience — it’s also about work ... tied to everyday life,” said another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko.

A blow to Russia’s AI ambitions

Yandex said it restored most key cloud services in the following days as it turned to other data centres in Russia. But the damage to the company’s AI development efforts is widely seen as massive and longer-lasting.

Yandex has invested in huge data centres as the global AI boom fuels demand for computing power. The company’s three supercomputers used to develop models are ranked among the top 500 in the world. Its most powerful computer — at the Sasovo data centre — was ranked 19th.

Yandex didn’t disclose the extent of the strikes’ consequences, but satellite images indicated its data centres sustained serious damage. Some observers noted that fires triggered by the attacks probably seriously damaged high-end chips and other key equipment.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

“With this kind of hit, it’s hard to expect that at least something was left intact — the data centres’ equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive,” Klimarev said. “Soot from the fire is bad for electronics.”

While Russia already lagged years behind the U.S. and China, “Ukraine’s drone strikes will likely still set back Russian AI efforts further,” said Connor Martin, an expert with the Council on Foreign Relations.

He said in a commentary that Russia likely will struggle to quickly replace the U.S.-designed Nvidia A100 chips powering Yandex’s supercomputers.

Klimarev also said the global deficit of high-end chips, combined with the sanctions on their delivery to Russia, will make repairs long and costly.

“I’m not sure it can be done in half a year, a year, or even at all,” he said.

items.title: Federal credit unions push Ottawa to fix merger and capital rules
items.description: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.content: <p>Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282819062614560.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.body:
Canada’s newest federal credit union is calling on Ottawa to overhaul its merger and regulatory framework, warning that without meaningful reform, smaller institutions cannot build national scale and Canadians will be left with a banking market dominated by a handful of major lenders.

In an opinion piece published in The Hill Times, Launi Skinner, CEO of Tru Cooperative Bank in Langley, British Columbia, outlined three priorities for the federal government:

  1. clearer merger regulations and appropriate tax treatment
  2. coordinated review processes across federal agencies
  3. capital requirements calibrated to an institution’s actual size and risk profile

“For far too long, Canadians have had limited choice when it comes to national banking options,” Skinner wrote.

Tru Cooperative Bank, formerly First West Credit Union, became federally regulated in April and currently serves approximately 290,000 members with approximately $21 billion in total assets and assets under administration.

In September, it announced a proposed merger with Ontario’s Libro Credit Union that would create an organization serving approximately 470,000 members with nearly $33 billion in combined assets, subject to member and regulatory approvals.

The case for a stronger middle tier

Canada’s national residential mortgage market carries more than $2.4 trillion in outstanding debt, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) data for December 2025, yet most credit unions remain regionally concentrated.

“Canada needs more institutions between those two ends of the market,” Skinner wrote — cooperatives with national capabilities and the local accountability that distinguishes them from publicly traded banks.

The appetite to fill that gap is already visible at the lender level. At MortgageFest Canada 2026, Bekim Merdita, head of sales and marketing at QuestBank, formerly Community Trust, described the institution’s positioning. 

“Community Trust, 50-year-old trust company. And really, at the end of last year, we got our banking licence — a Schedule 1 bank — and rebranded ourselves to Quest Bank. It gives us the ability to not just do mortgage products, but other products as well that serve the consumer and really start building a financial ecosystem for our consumer.”

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has signalled a less conservative approach to approving new banking entrants, and the regulator’s updated approvals framework launched in June aims to widen market access further.

For brokers navigating a more complex lender roster, regulatory inconsistency is already a top frustration. Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer of WealthOne Bank of Canada, told MortgageFest Canada 2026. 

"The biggest pain points that we’re hearing from brokers is the ever-changing policies, the ever-changing rules, the ever-changing processes that lenders are doing," he said. 

"Every single week a lender has changed how you submit a deal, what forms you need, what documents — and brokers are struggling to keep up."

What Ottawa needs to do

Skinner argued that mergers involving federal credit unions — requiring review by OSFI, the Competition Bureau, and the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC), alongside the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) and the Department of Finance — should not generate duplicative information requests or conflicting regulatory interpretations.

“No responsible cooperative leader is asking for weaker consumer protection or lower standards of safety and soundness,” she wrote.

“But equivalent standards do not always require identical requirements.”

She also called for proportionate capital rules, arguing requirements designed around systemically important banks divert management capacity away from cybersecurity, digital banking, and small-business lending at mid-sized cooperatives.

Federally regulated credit unions now hold approximately $47 billion of the $330 billion in total assets across Canadian credit unions nationally, according to the Canadian Credit Union Association (CCUA).

The Tru–Libro combination, if approved, would represent the sector’s most substantial attempt yet to fill the gap Skinner has identified, and the clearest test of whether Ottawa’s updated framework can deliver.

items.title: GTA High-Rise Sales Sink To A September Record Low
items.description:
Builders in the Greater Toronto Area sold 820 new low-rise homes in September, 17% above the 10-year average for the month. It’s the sixth month in a row low-rise sales have cleared that bar, which covers every month since the HST rebate program launched.

High-rise went the other way. Just 129 new high-rise units sold in September, according to new figures from the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD) and Altus Group, BILD’s official source for new home market data. That’s the lowest September on record for the segment, down 40% from September 2025 and 90% below the 10-year average. (BILD’s high-rise category includes units in low-, medium- and high-rise buildings, plus stacked townhouses.)

The low-rise surge isn’t enough to carry the market on its own. Total new home sales came to 949 in September. That’s up significantly from a year ago, and still 52% below the 10-year average of 1,978 units for the month.

Both segments are operating under the same program. BILD and Altus point to its rules around construction start and completion dates as the main obstacle keeping high-rise from taking part the way low-rise has. Altus also names a second problem.

“The high-rise sector remained plagued by undesirable inventory and program constraints centred on unattainable construction timelines,” said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group.

High-rise inventory inched up to 12,909 units in September, or roughly 49 months of supply based on average sales over the last 12 months. Low-rise inventory sits at 7,048 homes, or 11 months’ worth.

And within low-rise, buyers are reaching for different product types than they used to.

“In the low-rise market, we have seen a positive response to the HST rebate program with increased sales activity and greater interest in semi-detached homes and townhouses,” said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD. “More than half of September’s sales were in semis and townhomes, representing a shift from traditional levels.”

Pricing has moved on that side of the market, too. The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,246,764 in September, down 13.3% over the last 12 months. The high-rise benchmark held at $1,031,574, unchanged from a year ago. Both are gross prices that don’t reflect the HST rebate, so buyers who qualify would see an additional benefit.

Sherwood said the September high-rise numbers show the program rules need to change.

“The high-rise sales performance in September should be a wake-up call that there needs to be further measures and a modification of the program rules to allow the high-rise sector to better participate in the program, which would enable homebuyers in every segment of the housing market to benefit,” he said.

In Simcoe County, the split was starker still: 73 new low-rise homes sold in September at a weighted average price of $998,787, and not a single high-rise unit.

items._ogDesc: Parks Canada tells CTV News Ottawa that 2,917 employees will receive notices that their positions are “impacted by workforce adjustment” in the second round of workforce adjustment.
items.body:
Thousands of employees at Parks Canada will receive notices that their jobs are at risk as the federal department enters the “second period” of workforce adjustments.

Parks Canada tells CTV News Ottawa that 2,917 employees will receive notices that their positions will “impacted by workforce adjustment” in the weeks ahead.

The department is expecting to reduce full-time equivalent positions by approximately 500 positions through the workforce adjustments.

“Parks Canada has been working to modernize how it delivers programs and services to ensure they provide the greatest value to Canadians while supporting long-term sustainability,” Parks Canada said in an email Wednesday afternoon.

“Over the coming months, Parks Canada will implement organizational changes to align with available funding, modernize operations, strengthen field-based decision-making, and ensure it remains well positioned to deliver on our mandate into the future.”

Parks Canada says all employees “directly impacted by the decisions” will be informed directly by their director or field unit superintendent.

“Our focus on visitor service, conservation, and enabling memorable experiences remains unchanged,” the department said.

“Parks Canada will continue to focus on protecting the places entrusted to its care and ensuring they can be enjoyed by current and future generations.”

In June, Parks Canada entered its “first period of workforce adjustments,” with notices issued to public servants. The department did not disclose how many employees received a notice or how positions would be impacted in the first round of the workforce adjustment.

According to the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, Parks Canada employed 4,773 people as of March 31, 2026.

The federal government launched the workforce adjustment process in the Canada Strong Budget 2025 last November, which outlined the federal government’s plan to reduce the size of the federal public service by 28,000 positions by 2029, with 16,000 full-time equivalent positions eliminated through the comprehensive expenditure review.

As of Aug. 5, 25,368 employees and 1,146 executives in the federal public service had received workforce adjustment notices.

The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat says 9,438 federal public servants have been approved for early retirement packages.

items.title: When should you start collecting CPP and OAS?: Stan Wong
items.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A man looks over a brochures offering various retirement savings options Friday, February 3, 2012 in Montreal. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ryan Remiorz]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
items.body:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).

Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan.

Do you actually need the income?

Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn.

The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes.

Taxes can change the calculation

Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback.

For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320.

CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting.

Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient.

The financial reward for waiting

CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70.

OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70.

Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75.

How long must you live to come out ahead?

Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results.

According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report, a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89.

These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement.

A total wealth planning decision

There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense.

Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives.

The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security.

items.description:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers […]

The post Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: National Bank warns Canada’s housing market needs higher immigration and foreign buyers to clear a record inventory of unsold homes and avoid a demographic cliff.
items.body:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers to increase their immigration targets and reintroduce foreign buyers to help developers reduce inventory.

Canadian Real Estate In A Slump Despite Billions In Bailouts

The Great Canadian Real Estate Slump isn’t exactly news, but not everyone may be aware of how slow it’s been. Over 1 in 4 (28%) newly completed homes remain unsold, charting new territory for excess supply. “The inventory of completed and unsold housing units across all census metropolitan areas stands at 20,700 units, its highest level since records began in 1990,” warns the bank.

Existing homes aren’t doing much better. Seasonally adjusted sales saw a monthly drop of 2.3% in September, sliding 13% below the 10-year average. While Canadian home prices are now in the biggest correction on record, the almost 5-year slump only rolled back 13 months of price gains. That’s with taxpayer-backed bailouts.

“This demonstrates that the market is so weak that it requires public support,” writes National Bank.

Policymakers aren’t dabbling in support either—they’re fully immersed in the practice. The bank cites Ontario’s $1.3 billion bailout to help investors buy 2,200 unsold Toronto condos. They also cite Ottawa and British Columbia’s $1.45 billion program for roughly the same number of condos. These programs are massive, but even taxpayer-funded bulk buying isn’t enough to clear the backlog.

The bank urges policymakers to drum up more demand. Not from the young adults struggling with shelter costs. They can’t afford to buy a home. They’re calling on Ottawa to look beyond its borders to support prices. Seriously.

Big Six Bank Calls For Higher Immigration To Improve Demand

Canadian real estate prices surged from 2020 and finally peaked in March 2022. That occurred during the pandemic’s population slump, when population growth plummeted to near historic lows. Canada ramped up immigration to unprecedented levels as the slump kicked off. Despite a timing mismatch, reduced immigration is often cited as extending the downturn. The narrative was reinforced by StatCan’s population estimates that revealed a historic contraction. However, that contraction also didn’t happen.

The agency’s recent revisions show the 0.5% y/y decline reported at the start of 2026 was actually 0.5% growth. Ottawa’s plan to reduce non-permanent residents (NPR) to 5% of the population by 2027 is also unlikely. Not only did policymakers delay the target by a year, but NPRs currently represent 6.7% of the population. Canada needs to lose roughly 750,000 NPRs by the end of next year to make those numbers work. Still, the Big Six Bank is concerned.

Reducing NPRs to 5% of the total population will slow total growth to 0.2% in 2027 and 0.1% in 2028, notes the bank. They warn that sticking to the target will mean more downward pressure on housing. “In that context, we believe Ottawa should recalibrate its immigration policy through a targeted and gradual increase in immigration levels,” says National Bank.

Canadians Can’t Afford Homes? Sell Them To Foreign Investors

Canada’s foreign homebuyer restrictions are set to expire in a few months. “The ban on foreign home purchases, which expires on January 1, 2027, should not be extended but rather replaced by a more flexible policy,” explains National Bank.

Whether Canada will renew the moratorium is unclear, but policymakers aren’t fond of the measures. They began to quietly ease foreign buyer restrictions just 86 days after boasting of passing the ban. Canada has since elected Prime Minister Mark Carney, and while he hasn’t addressed the ban directly, the bank notes he recently laid the groundwork for a “controlled increase” in the population.

One of his key fundraisers in BC has been a little more vocal about foreign capital returning to housing. Shortly after PM Carney was elected, Vancouver’s “condo king” said he was working with the PM to drum up foreign capital for rentals.

National Bank sees foreign buyers as one of the only ways developers can sell the homes they built. “We believe it should not be renewed in its current form and that a more flexible model—such as Australia’s, which notably allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes—would help reduce the inventory of unsold housing,” argues the bank.

The bank’s take seems tone-deaf, but the implications are more disturbing. RBC recently found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41, 12 years later than current owners did. Separately, they found parents are increasingly helping their adult kids pay bills—a trend most parents attribute to a soaring cost of living rather than poor money management.

Canada’s young adults have been locked out of the housing market. For years they were told that more supply would close the gap, and building more would finally bring prices down. After taxpayers footed the bill to accelerate construction, the narrative abruptly shifted: prices can’t fall further because developers can’t make the math work. Since young adults can’t afford these prices, we suddenly need more temporary residents to support attractive rents that developers can pitch to foreign landlords.

items.content: <p>Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada rate jump could cut the recovery short</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282053551425211.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada rate jump could cut the recovery short
items.body:
Ontario’s housing market is set for a modest recovery in 2027, with Desjardins Group forecasting a near-5% rise in existing home sales. However, a looming Bank of Canada rate increase could erode the affordability gains brokers are only starting to see.

In its Ontario Housing Outlook, Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman projects provincial resales will reach about 167,000 units next year, up 4.7%, while the average price edges up 2.4% to roughly $825,000.

Lower prices, rising incomes, first-time buyer supports and pent-up demand should pull buyers back, though activity will stay well below long-term norms.

What a Bank of Canada hike would mean for Ontario borrowers

Desjardins expects two quarter-point increases, starting in late October. The central bank has held its overnight rate at 2.25% since October 2025, and its next decision lands October 28 as markets price in a growing likelihood of Bank of Canada rate hikes.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, saw the same signals at MortgageFest 2026.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points,” he said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, is less convinced. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he told the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, where he also urged brokers to steer clients toward the five-year fixed mortgage.

Daren King of National Bank of Canada and Penelope Graham of Ratehub .ca say five-year fixed-rate mortgages have fallen to a record-low share of new lending as more borrowers opt for variable-rate and shorter-term products. https://t.co/CVKUTrrUL5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

First-time buyers step into the gap

Toronto’s condo slump remains the biggest drag. Only 525 condo units were started in the City of Toronto in the first nine months of 2026, against nearly 14,000 a year over the previous decade, the report said – a collapse that has left many presale condo buyers facing appraisal shortfalls and lost deposits.

Temporary HST relief of up to $130,000 and Toronto development-charge cuts of 40% to 60% through August 2029 aim to restart activity.

For end users, the reset is an opening. “For people who actually need to buy real estate for their own use, I think that’s really the best time to get into the market,” Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada, said at MortgageFest.

Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, sees the same shift.

“With the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines are finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown,” she said.

Desjardins projects housing starts will rise about 6% to nearly 65,000 units in 2027, still more than 30% below 2021 and 2022 levels. Norman flagged Canada-US trade tensions and Middle East-driven oil prices as key risks.

items.body:
How much should governments pay to acquire land?

Under the BC NDP, the province has acquired several private properties for public use, paying what some industry sources describe as an unusual premium.

In fall 2025, the province announced that it had allocated $26 million to the Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique to acquire 3044 Pratt St., Abbotsford, for a Francophone school. Provincial transaction data records a purchase price from a subsidiary of Abbotsford’s Azure Properties Group of $24.6 million, or $2 million an acre (leaving $1.4 million to cover transaction and closing costs).

On Jan. 29, the province acquired a 40-acre property at 1320 McKenzie Rd., Abbotsford, from a subsidiary of Richmond’s Panatch Group for $27.8 million, or $695,000 an acre. The property was used to grow vegetables, but Infrastructure BC plans to build a new Plant and Animal Health Centre on the site in partnership with the B.C. Ministry of Agriculture and Food.

On March 31, Crown corporation BC Hydro acquired a 21.75-acre parcel of vacant industrial land at 2161 Caribou Drive, Langford, from Vancouver-based developers Strand and Bastion Development Corp. for $52.5 million, or an average of $2.4 million an acre.

Howard Chai, who broke news of the deal at The Realist, noted that the “very specific” real estate needs of public entities often result in them appearing to pay more for sites than what other, less constrained parties might.

In the case of the school site in Abbotsford, industry sources indicate that the price was well above not just the $9.8 million value the BC Assessment assigned it on July 1, 2025, but also previous offers by private developers.

One well-known Vancouver developer who spoke to Western Investor on condition of anonymity, considered acquiring the property after it returned to market in fall 2022. Plans filed with the city at the time called for 130 townhomes on a developable area of seven acres. Pricing guidance stood at $24 million.

However, the site’s challenging topography, marked by steep slopes and fish-bearing streams, left just 3.5 acres suitable for development in the view of the developer. It couldn’t justify a price greater than $10 million.

An accepted offer in the range of $18 million ultimately came through, but during the due diligence process the purchaser reduced the offer to $15.5 million—again, because of site considerations. The deal collapsed.

An industry source familiar with the details—also speaking anonymously—called the price the province paid “crazy” and “a ridiculous amount of money,” especially for a property that would need to be rezoned before a school could be built.

“It’s a massive risk,” the source said, noting that Abbotsford has historically been reluctant to tweak its Official Community Plan to accommodate new uses within established zones.

Similarly, the province paid several times Farm Credit Canada’s reported regional average of $104,600 for agricultural parcels last year to acquire the farmland for the new Plant and Animal Health Centre. With farmland values in B.C. declining over the past 18 months, the province’s premium looks even more egregious.

While the purchase price was “well below” the prices of nearby retail or industrial properties, the site was purchased as actively farmed land within the Agricultural Land Reserve that would require a non-farm use application.

“Why the province paid so dearly for it, relative to what Panatch paid in 2020, is a bit of a mystery,” said Paul Richter, director of market analytics with CoStar. “They did go through the process to get ALC approval to subdivide into two parcels, and for ‘non-farm use’ approvals to permit the [Plant and Animal Health] Centre. This could have added value, for the right buyer. In this case, the only buyer that would have likely stepped up, stepped up. The province.”

The spending practices of other levels of government offer a point of comparison for the province’s land acquisitions.

The Department of National Defence acquired two multi-family properties on Vancouver Island last year to house personnel. A newly built 37-unit property at 244 Island Highway in View Royal traded in early October 2025 for $23.4 million, or an average of $631,622 per door unit—the most expensive multi-family transaction in Greater Victoria last year, according to CBRE Ltd. statistics.

Near CFB Comox, DND bought a 52-unit property at 574 Cumberland Rd., Courtenay, from Simba Investments Ltd. for $19.1 million. The purchase price averaged $367,308 a door—a premium versus the Mid-Island average at mid-year as reported by CBRE of $200,938 per door.

Within the Lower Mainland, the City of Coquitlam paid $3 million—or an average of $16.7 million per acre—in August 2025 for a 0.18-acre medium-density residential development site at 570 Austin Ave., Coquitlam.

The various government transactions, all completed within a few months of one another and involving different asset types, show a willingness to spend well beyond what the private sector would pay.

“It’s definitely a trend,” said the industry source familiar with the history of the Pratt Road site. “With half the developers I have done business with over the years, it’s well known that if they’re moving forward with a property, it’s because they’ve done their due diligence and they know that they can make money doing this. And they do that because they’re responsible for their own private capital and don’t want to lose money.”

items.title: Global mobility’s compliance blind spots are costing organizations
items.description: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.content: <p>As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0287_639281217985765444.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.body:
The way Canadian organizations manage their people’s movement across borders has changed fundamentally – and most HR teams haven’t kept pace. As cross-border work shifts from structured international assignments to informal arrangements involving remote work, frequent business travel, and digital nomad arrangements, compliance obligations have multiplied without a corresponding evolution in governance.

The risks are unlike anything the industry has previously navigated, says Jack Kim, Partner in the Toronto office of Fragomen, a global immigration services firm. “The global mobility environment is quite in flux and you have a lot of tensions grappling against each other,” says Kim. He says that demand for global talent is surging in priority sectors including defence, energy, and infrastructure, but political headwinds at home and abroad are complicating access to that talent as enforcement tightens worldwide.

The data underscores the problem. According to global workforce management firm ECA’s Global Mobility Now 2026 study, two-thirds of global employers have no formal process for reviewing compliance implications, such as immigration limits or internal company thresholds. With nearly half of organizations in the study expecting business travel to increase and international remote work to grow over the next two years, that gap is only widening.

When informal mobility becomes a liability

Compliance problems rarely begin with a policy failure, says Kim. More often, they start with a routine trip. An employee travels repeatedly to a client in the U.S. A specialist is dispatched to an overseas facility under no formal assignment structure. None of these situations looks like a traditional global mobility file – but each can trigger payroll obligations, immigration requirements and corporate tax exposure simultaneously, he says.

“Especially on the tax front, it’s a pain in the butt to track where are my employees on any given day,” Kim says, noting that technology helps but there are also cultural questions to be considered. “And that has increased the need for employers to be able to do exactly what governments are trying to do. Where is a person on any given day? Are there a certain number of days that trigger a tax complication or an immigration complication as well? And then how do I do it?”

When individual non-compliance goes undetected, the consequences rarely stay contained. Kim points to a recent U.S. enforcement action at a battery plant in Atlanta involving a Korean company, as a cautionary example of how quickly a workforce issue becomes a geopolitical one. “Hundreds of people were apprehended at the same time, and it caused lots of news stories and consternation from governments,” he says. “It turned into a bilateral issue and a geopolitical issue.”

Kim cautions Canadian organizations against treating such scenarios as distinctly American. “This could also happen in different countries as well because the number one question, especially in countries that are facing populist-type movements, is that they don’t want people to be working illegally inside their country, and no political party wants to own that as part of a scandal.”

The case for centralized mobility governance

The decentralized approach many organizations default to – leaving individual entities or regional HR teams to manage their own immigration processes independently – is no longer adequate. Leaving immigration or compliance processes siloed across business units or provinces is a structural liability at this stage of regulatory complexity, according to Kim. “Those days are probably over because of all the complexities that you have to think about, and the dependencies between everything that happens,” he says.

Greater visibility at the executive level is equally important. Kim uses the example of a travel ban enacted by Canada during a public health emergency in Africa from Ebola to illustrate how a mobility gap becomes a leadership crisis overnight. “If you don’t know where your people are, and if you have a facility in the Democratic Republic of Congo, then you need to know who’s there right now visiting, and that immediately becomes a C-suite issue, whether you like it or not.”

The model Kim advocates is cross-functional by design, integrating immigration, tax, travel management, technology and HR business partners into a unified framework. Organizations building cross-border workforce compliance frameworks that address immigration, tax, and travel risk, as well as balance global hiring with cross-border compliance obligations, are better placed to manage the dependencies that determine whether international moves succeed or stall, he says.

“Those things should be thought of at the front end of decision-making, not at the back end,” Kim says. “Be proactive about these things, increasing visibility within your own companies, having policies in place and game planning, crisis control – because more often than not, as we've seen with the wars going on in the Middle East and in Ukraine, there's some more strategic planning that needs to be done and you cannot be reactive anymore.”

Canada’s regulatory reset and what it means for HR

Canada’s immigration system is itself in transition. Tighter temporary resident targets and the pending transfer of International Mobility Program (IMP) compliance oversight from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) signal a more enforcement-focused posture from Ottawa for employers navigating the process of hiring foreign workers.

Kim describes the recalibration that began in 2024 as “in spirit necessary” – a response to documented system fraud, housing shortages, and strained school capacity. But he warns that the recalibration must be carefully managed. “What we need to do as a country going forward is to think of things in a much more intentional and calculated manner, strategic,” he says.

He points to a recent government initiative prioritizing permanent residence pathways for high-wage workers as a constructive signal, but stresses that Canada’s capacity needs make continued access to international talent non-negotiable. “We want to build submarines, but we’re contracting a foreign company to build them for us for the next 30 years,” he says. “If we want to build pipelines, then we need people to help us build those because the talent doesn’t all reside in Canada.”

With below-replacement birth rates now recorded across 37 of 38 Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries according to the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance 2025 report, the competition for skilled talent will only intensify. HR leaders monitoring Canada’s evolving immigration policy landscape and its impact on workforce strategy should treat government engagement – through their own C-suite or government relations functions – as a core part of their long-term planning, according to Kim.

“We’re going to be competing for the same people across the world for years to come,” he says.

Duty of care in a volatile world

As geopolitical risk becomes a standard feature of the global operating environment, duty of care for internationally mobile employees has shifted from a compliance consideration to a strategic imperative. Kim, who was involved in emergency evacuation efforts during the Taliban’s seizure of Kabul in 2021, knows precisely what inadequate planning looks like. “That was a real frantic couple of weeks when we were trying to get people out of the country,” he says.

Knowing where employees are, what travel authorizations they hold, and where they can be safely relocated is foundational. Organizations can plan for global immigration and labour mobility trends in advance – mapping visa-free travel options, identifying jurisdictions where an entity can provide temporary shelter and defining what a safe relocation pathway looks like before a crisis demands one. HR teams developing proactive duty-of-care and crisis response programs for internationally mobile employees are increasingly setting the standard expected by both regulators and the workforce itself.

As enforcement intensifies globally – such as stricter border rules that could impact business travellers – Kim says the penalties for non-compliance will follow. “Companies are more in the crosshairs too,” he says, pointing to major corporations in the U.S. that have faced restrictions on sponsoring foreign workers following fraud-related allegations. The reputational damage, he notes, arrives well before any verdict.

“Whether those allegations have been proven or not is a different thing, but once you’re in the headlines, you’re in the headlines,” says Kim. “And so these things will likely be used more at a higher level to cut things off at the pass.”

items.title: Ottawa is selling homes fast – but building the wrong kind
items.description: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.content: <p>A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281937065157840.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.body:
Ottawa’s new home market posted its strongest September in recent memory, with 521 sales recorded. That's an 81.5% increase from the 287 transactions closed in September 2025, according to data from the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association (GOHBA) and PMA Brethour Realty Group.

Month-over-month, activity climbed 12.3% from August’s 464 units. Year-to-date, 4,078 new homes have sold in Ottawa through September, up 53.8% from 2,652 at the same point last year.

Supply gap persists despite record sales pace

Housing starts in Ottawa are up 14% in 2026, with 8,169 homes under construction compared with 7,168 in the same period last year, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

However, the gains have not kept pace with demand for ownership housing. Much of that pipeline is weighted toward rental, raising the prospect that Ottawa’s affordability recovery could go into reverse if the ownership supply gap continues to widen.

Jason Burggraaf, Executive Director of the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association in Ontario, said September’s gains carry an important caveat.

“September’s sales are encouraging, but CMHC’s latest report shows Ottawa still faces a widening housing supply gap, with much of its construction activity concentrated in rentals,” Burggraaf said.

“Improving affordability means supporting more ownership housing too. Finalizing the development charge reduction agreement is an immediate opportunity to lower building costs, and we’re pushing for a timely resolution so some 2026 construction can benefit.”

The concern echoes comments Burggraaf made on Ottawa’s August new home sales results, when he cautioned, “Governments need to ensure that the way we fund growth doesn’t add costs that put those homes further out of reach.”

Geographically, Ottawa’s west end captured 43% of September sales, with the south at 40%, together accounting for 83% of all transactions.

The east recorded 15% and Central Ottawa 2%. Townhomes led all product types at 44%, followed by single-detached homes at 35% and condo townhomes at 20%.

Development charge relief within reach

City council approved a plan in July to reduce development charges by 54% over three years, tied to a joint federal-Ontario infrastructure fund.

Under that framework, charges on single-family and semi-detached homes inside the Greenbelt would fall to $25,752, with suburban builds set at $28,781.

Development charges are one-time fees levied on new residential properties to fund growth-related capital infrastructure.

The push to finalise the agreement comes as Canada’s housing affordability reached a four-year best in Q1 2026, according to RBC Economics, with the national aggregate measure falling to 53% of pre-tax median household income required to cover ownership costs.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence climbs, but housing optimism lags
items.description: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.content: <p>Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281927714349803.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence firmed in mid-October, yet Canadians’ outlook for home values, the measure that matters most to mortgage brokers, still sits well below its historical norm.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) reached 51.68 for the four weeks ending October 16, up from 49.86 a month earlier.

The weekly gauge is compiled from a rolling telephone survey of 1,016 Canadians. It sits above the neutral 50 mark but below its long-run average of 54.66 since 2008.

Almost all of the improvement came from the forward-looking side of the survey.

"The improvement was driven largely by brighter expectations: that sub-index climbed to 48.41 from 44.82. Pocketbook confidence, covering personal finances and job security, was broadly unchanged at 54.94," said Nik Nanos, chief data scientist at Nanos Research.

"Even so, overall confidence remains below its long-run average of 54.66, suggesting Canadians are feeling somewhat better, but remain cautious about the economic outlook as the year moves ahead."

What do Canadians expect from home prices?

The Expectations Index combines views on the economy with views on neighbourhood real estate, and the housing component remains soft.

Just 29.10% of respondents expect local home values to rise over the next six months. That is below the 2026 average of 34.28% and the long-run average of 39.76%.

Another 45.65% expect prices to hold, while 19.96% anticipate a decline.

Household finances offer little cushion. Only 11.03% said their personal finances improved over the past year, compared with 37.91% who said they were worse off.

British Columbia was the only region in net-negative territory, at 46.02. Ontario sat just under neutral at 49.91.

A new international research by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) revealed that Canada’s inflation-adjusted home prices more than doubled between 2005 and 2025, rising 101% and outpacing every major peer country.

Fausto Gaudio of IC Savings argues that home prices remain too disconnected from incomes, making it increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to enter the market and highlighting the need for a broader affordability reset. https://t.co/3PehdHgrJn — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

How the confidence data fits the Bank of Canada rate call

Nanos said the Expectations Index has tracked year-over-year GDP growth with a 0.82 correlation on a six-month lag, and that the data has been cited in the Bank of Canada’s Monetary Policy Report. That makes the reading a timely input one week before the central bank’s October 28 decision. The overnight rate has stood at 2.25% since October 2025.

Most of the bank economists calling for an October 28 rate hold point to September’s inflation data.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group, addressed those figures amid rising business inflation expectations in the Bank’s latest survey.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has urged brokers to recommend the five-year fixed over variable. He was direct about the risk of tightening. 

“I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he noted.
